title: Nara Japan
capsule: The Nara period (710–794) takes its name from the first permanent Japanese capital at Heijō-kyō (modern Nara), modeled on the Tang Chinese capital Chang'an, to which the court moved from Fujiwara-kyō in 710 under Empress Genmei. The era saw the compilation of Japan's earliest chronicles—the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720)—as well as the Manyōshū poetry anthology, and the construction of Tōdai-ji temple with its monumental bronze Great Buddha (Daibutsu), completed 752. Smallpox epidemics in the 730s devastated the population and generated destabilizing political crises; the capital was moved to Nagaoka-kyō in 784 and definitively to Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794, ending the Nara period.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Nara state's administrative geography is well-documented in the Taihō and Yōrō codes, though effective provincial control in northern Honshu (Emishi territories) was contested and frontier boundaries are approximate.
